analysis.one_liner: Toughens federal rules on lead in drinking water, requiring public disclosure of lead service lines and a lower lead limit.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2019 and referred to a House committee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2021 without a markup or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the EPA to rewrite its lead and copper drinking water rules. Water systems would have to report test results publicly, map where lead service lines are, say who owns those lines, investigate any home that tests above the lead limit, replace whole lead lines rather than half of them, and cut the allowable lead level in drinking water from 15 parts per billion to 10 by the end of 2020 and 5 by 2026.
analysis.who_benefits: Families drinking from lead pipes, especially households with children and pregnant women, who would get faster notice of contamination, on-site investigations, plain-language public data about their water system, and full lead service line replacement instead of partial replacement that can temporarily make lead levels worse.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with lead pipes, especially kids

how_it_helps.text: Water systems would have to make test results, lead service line maps, and line-ownership records publicly available in plain language, with a mail-delivery option for people without internet access.

When a sample exceeds the lead or copper action level, the water system or local health department would have to do an on-site investigation within 10 business days and notify the affected household within 2 days.

The EPA's sampling protocol would have to prohibit techniques that minimize lead detection, prioritize high-risk buildings including homes of pregnant women and children, and require testing at all taps in schools and child care centers served by the system.
The allowable lead action level in drinking water would drop to 10 parts per billion by the end of 2020 and 5 parts per billion by 2026.

analysis.who_pays: Public water utilities, whose costs for testing, inventories, investigations, and full line replacement would likely be passed to ratepayers through water bills; also federal, state, and local agencies administering the new rules.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls on water utilities, and utilities typically recover such costs from customers through water bills, so the mandate's costs would partly land on the same households it protects.

Full-service-line replacement, inventories of every service line, and 10-day on-site investigations are expensive and logistically demanding, and the bill did not specify new federal funding to pay for them.

Homeowners can opt to have their address shown only by block number and street name, which somewhat limits the transparency of the public maps, though the exception does not apply to child care centers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health upside is substantial: lead in drinking water causes permanent harm to children's development, and the bill's transparency, testing, and lower action level directly target that harm. The real costs are money and logistics for water systems, which ratepayers would partly shoulder, and the bill's lack of dedicated funding is a fair criticism. On balance the benefits to exposed families clearly outweigh the compliance costs, though a better bill would have paired the mandates with money to pay for line replacement.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee in July 2019 and never received a markup or a floor vote before that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Kildee, a Democrat from Michigan, introduced the bill on July 10, 2019.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day and to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change the next day.
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote appears in the action history before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill drew only one cosponsor during its entire run.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Water utilities are better off because the bill died, since they avoided new quarterly reporting, public inventories, mandated investigations, and full lead service line replacement. Households with lead pipes are worse off, since no action-level change or disclosure requirement from this bill took effect through it.

for.name: Rep. Dan Kildee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tighten EPA lead and copper drinking water rules, drawing on his Michigan constituents' experience with lead contamination.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or sent it to the floor during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no party split is on the record; both the sponsor and the single cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed quarterly testing reports, public service-line inventories, mandated on-site investigations, and full lead service line replacement on water systems. Their interest in avoiding those compliance costs runs against the public's interest in clean, disclosed data on lead in their water.
Mandatory full replacement of lead service lines would have created a large volume of replacement work for contractors, serving the same goal as protecting residents from lead.
Departments would gain a defined role investigating contaminated homes, but must complete those investigations within 10 business days with no new funding specified in the bill.
